cause_set.author: dee-mensah
cause_set.summary: config: standardise table keys on the _NAME suffix (ORDERS_TABLE -> ORDERS_TABLE_NAME)

cause_set.author: dee-mensah
cause_set.summary: iam: collapse per-table orders ARNs into one prefix (orders-prod -> orders-*)

mechanism: The 09:34 ConfigMap edit renamed the key ORDERS_TABLE to ORDERS_TABLE_NAME in the prod overlay. The 09:35 rollout restarted orders-api pods, which re-read their environment and no longer found ORDERS_TABLE. orders-api fell through to the hardcoded default in app/config.py, DEFAULT_ORDERS_TABLE = 'orders-staging', written during the 2023 bring-up. Before 09:12 that write would have been refused: the IAM policy scoped orders-api to arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/orders-prod, so a PutItem against orders-staging returned AccessDenied and would have paged within minutes. The 09:12 Terraform change widened that resource to arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/orders-* , which permits orders-staging. The write therefore succeeded, returned 201, and produced no error, no latency change and no infrastructure alert. Production orders landed in the staging table until the business metric orders_created was noticed 40 minutes later.
short_term: Stop the bleeding by restoring the ORDERS_TABLE key in the prod overlay and rolling out orders-api -- but only after step 1 of the order of operations below. Do not revert the ConfigMap first.
long_term: Remove the DEFAULT_ORDERS_TABLE fallback from orders-api/app/config.py so a missing ORDERS_TABLE fails loudly at startup instead of silently selecting another environment's table. Add a startup assertion that the resolved table name matches the deployment's environment. Guard rail for the class: require a consumer-impact check on ConfigMap key renames in platform-config (the reverse index already knows who reads each key), and forbid cross-environment ARN prefixes in shared IAM modules.
order_of_operations: Export every row written to orders-staging since 09:35 to durable storage. The table has a 24h TTL and these are real customer orders.
Restore the ORDERS_TABLE key in platform-config overlays/prod/orders.yaml and sync.
Roll out orders-api and verify new writes are landing in orders-prod.
Re-scope the IAM policy in platform-iac modules/iam/dynamodb.tf from orders-* back to orders-prod.
Reconcile the exported records into orders-prod, de-duplicating on order_id.
rollback_hazard: orders-staging carries a 24h TTL. Reverting the ConfigMap first, without exporting, redirects new writes correctly but leaves roughly 40 minutes of real customer orders (~4,000 rows) sitting in a table that will expire them permanently. The obvious rollback destroys data. Export before reverting.

direct: orders-api -- writing to the wrong destination since 09:35
orders-staging -- now holds production customer data it was never scoped for
indirect: All 14 services consuming the shared IAM module in platform-iac environments/prod/main.tf now hold a widened orders-* grant

security_implications: The IAM wildcard remains live after the functional fix. arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/orders-* lets production orders-api credentials read and write any table whose name begins with orders-, including orders-staging and any future orders-* table. No service requires this. It must be re-scoped and filed separately from the incident fix, because correcting the ConfigMap makes the symptom disappear while leaving the over-broad grant in place. Separately: production customer records now sit in a staging table with weaker access controls and should be treated as a data-handling incident.

confidence.would_change_my_mind: Evidence that orders-api was restarted after 09:34 with ORDERS_TABLE present in its environment -- that would break the link between the rename and the fallback. Also: a pre-09:12 authorization log showing a successful write to orders-staging, which would mean the guard rail was never in place and the IAM change is not a cause.
confidence.cheapest_disambiguating_query: Replay the pre-09:12 IAM policy against a PutItem to orders-staging and confirm it returns AccessDenied. Five seconds, and it separates the two-cause explanation from the one-cause one.

verification.observed: AccessDenied: implicit deny, no statement matches. Replaying the post-change policy against the same call returns Allow via arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/orders-*.
verification.expected: AccessDenied under the pre-change policy; Allow under the post-change policy
